full_judgment:
This Rule calls in question the judgment and order dated 28-11-95 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Netrokona in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 192 of 1981 affirming the judgment and order dated 20-4-1981 disallowing pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 8. Mr Santi Ranjan Karmaker, the learned Counsel appearing for the pre-emptee-opposite party No. 1, on the other hand, submits that since the statutory requirement of law under section 90 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is that a person seeking pre-emption must be a person to whom pre-emption may be allowed under the law, it was squarely on the shoulder of the petitioner to make a positive assertion in his pre-emption application as well as in his evidence that the land under pre-emption if added to his existing holding it shall not exceed the statutory limit. There being no such assertion either in the pre-emption application or in the evidence of the pre-emptor, it is evident that he has failed to fulfil the requirement of law to be entitled to an order of pre-emption and, as such, the learned Court of appeal below did not commit any error of law in passing the impugned judgment. 

 9. Mr AHM Ziauddin Ahmed, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner, has placed before me the judgments of the Courts below. From the judgment of the trial Court it appears that the learned Munsif dismissed the petitioner's case on two grounds: (1) on the ground of limitation and (2) on the ground that the pre-emptor did not deposit the cost of improvement along with the pre-emption application. From the judgment of the learned Court of appeal below it appears that the learned Subordinate Judge did not agree with the learned Munsif in so far as it relates to deposit of improvement cost along with the pre-emption application. It is to be noted in this connection that section 96 of SAT Act does no make any provision for depositing improvement cost along with the pre-emption application. The cost of improvement, if claimed, is to be determined by the Court at the trial on taking evidence. So, it is inconceivable as to why for non-deposit of the improvement cost at the time of filing the pre-emption case, which is yet to be determined by the Court on taking evidence, pre-emption could be refused. The learned Court of appeal below is justified in reversing the finding of the learned Munsif on this count. So far as the finding of the learned Court of appeal below on the question of section of 90 of the SAT Act is concerned, it is true that the pre-emptor petitioner did not make any statement in his pre-emption application that if the land under pre-emption is added to the existing holding under his possession it will not exceed the statutory limit of holding of land set by section 90 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and he did not state anything in his evidence to this effect but, nonetheless, the pre-emptee-opposite party also never raised this question either in the written objection or in his evidence before the Court as a result of which neither party adduced any evidence on this point. Mr AHM Ziauddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate, his referred to me the case of Md Matiur Rahman vs. Md Iman Ali and others reported in 1981 BLD (AD) 280 in which their Lordships held that although there is no dispute to the proposition of law that a person seeking pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act must show that he is a person entitled to purchase or acquire land within the maximum ceiling as set out in section 90 of the SAT Act but mere omission to make an assertion in his application or to adduce evidence to this effect, in the absence of any averment to the contrary, will not render his application liable to be dismissed. It therefore, follows that if no objection has been raised at any stage of the trial the pre-emptor should be given an opportunity to lead evidence on this point when the question is raised.
